In order to reconcile economic development with mitigating carbon emissions, developing countries need particular support.
This would be both financial and technical.
The IPCC found that accelerated support would also tackle inequities in financial and economic vulnerability to climate change.
One way to achieve this is the Kyoto Protocol's ___E:Clean Development Mechanism U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clean_Development_Mechanism)___ (CDM).
Climate change mitigation policies can have a large and complex impact on the socio-economic status of individuals and countries This can be both positive and negative.
It is important to design policies well and make them inclusive.
Otherwise climate change mitigation measures can impose higher financial costs on poor households.

An evaluation was conducted on 1,500 climate policy interventions made between 1998 and 2022.  The interventions took place in 41 countries and across 6 continents, which together contributed 81% of the world's total emissions as of 2019. The evaluation found 63 successful interventions that resulted in significant emission reductions; the total CO 2 release averted by these interventions was between 0.6 and 1.8 billion metric tonnes.

The study focused on interventions with at least 4.5% emission reductions, but the researchers noted that meeting the reductions required by the Paris Agreement would require 23 billion metric tonnes per year. Generally, carbon pricing was found to be most effective in ___E:developed countries U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Developed_country)___ , while regulation was most effective in the ___E:developing countries U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Developing_country)___ .
Complementary policy mixes benefited from synergies, and were mostly found to be more effective interventions than the implementation of isolated policies.
The ___E:OECD U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/OECD)___ recognise 48 distinct climate mitigation policies suitable for implementation at national level.
Broadly, these can be categorised into three types: market based instruments, non market based instruments and other policies.

Emissions taxes These often require domestic emitters to pay a fixed fee or tax for every tonne of CO 2 emissions they release into the atmosphere.  : 4123 ___E:Methane emissions U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Methane_emissions)___ from fossil fuel extraction are also occasionally taxed.
But methane and nitrous oxide from agriculture are typically not subject to tax.  Removing unhelpful subsidies: Many countries provide subsidies for activities that affect emissions.

For example, significant ___E:fossil fuel subsidies U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fossil_fuel_subsidies)___ are present in many countries.  ___E:Phasing-out fossil fuel subsidies U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fossil_fuel_phase-out#Phase-out_of_fossil_fuel_subsidies)___ is crucial to address the climate crisis.
It must however be done carefully to avoid protests  and making poor people poorer.
Creating helpful subsidies : Creating subsidies and financial incentives.
One example is ___E:energy subsidies U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Energy_subsidy)___ to support clean generation which is not yet commercially viable such as tidal power.
Tradable permits : A ___E:permit system U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbon_emission_trading)___ can limit emissions.  : 415
Imposing additional costs on greenhouse gas emissions can make fossil fuels less competitive and accelerate investments into low-carbon sources of energy.

A growing number of countries raise a fixed ___E:carbon tax U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbon_tax)___ or participate in dynamic ___E:carbon emission trading U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbon_emission_trading)___ (ETS) systems.
In 2021, more than 21% of global greenhouse gas emissions were covered by a carbon price.
This was a big increase from earlier due to the introduction of the ___E:Chinese national carbon trading scheme U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_national_carbon_trading_scheme)___ .  : 23
Trading schemes offer the possibility to limit emission allowances to certain reduction targets.
However, an oversupply of allowances keeps most ETS at low price levels around $10 with a low impact.

This includes the Chinese ETS which started with $7/tCO 2 in 2021.  One exception is the ___E:European Union Emission Trading Scheme U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Union_Emission_Trading_Scheme)___ where prices began to rise in 2018. They reached about €80/tCO 2 in 2022.  This results in additional costs of about €0.04/KWh for coal and €0.02/KWh for gas combustion for electricity, depending on the ___E:emission intensity U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emission_intensity)___ . [citation needed] Industries which have high energy requirements and high emissions often pay only very low energy taxes, or even none at all.  : 11–80

While this is often part of national schemes, ___E:carbon offsets and credits U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbon_offsets_and_credits)___ can be part of a voluntary market as well such as on the international market.

Notably, the company ___E:Blue Carbon U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Carbon_(company))___ of the ___E:UAE U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UAE)___ has bought ownership over an area equivalent to the United Kingdom to be preserved in return for carbon credits.

___E:International cooperation U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_cooperation)___ is considered a critical enabler for climate action  : 52 while conflicts generally hamper it.  Almost all countries are parties to the ___E:United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_Framework_Convention_on_Climate_Change)___ (UNFCCC).
The ultimate objective of the UNFCCC is to stabilise atmospheric concentrations of greenhouse gases at a level that would prevent dangerous human interference with the climate system.
Although not designed for this purpose, the ___E:Montreal Protocol U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montreal_Protocol)___ has benefited climate change mitigation efforts.

The Montreal Protocol is an international treaty that has successfully reduced emissions of ___E:ozone-depleting substances U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ozone-depleting_substance)___ such as ___E:CFCs U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chlorofluorocarbon)___ .
These are also greenhouse gases.
Historically efforts to deal with climate change have taken place at a multinational level.

They involve attempts to reach a consensus decision at the United Nations, under the ___E:United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_Framework_Convention_on_Climate_Change)___ (UNFCCC).
This is the dominant approach historically of engaging as many international governments as possible in taking action on a worldwide public issue.

The ___E:Montreal Protocol U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montreal_Protocol)___ in 1987 is a precedent that this approach can work. But some critics say the top-down framework of only utilising the UNFCCC consensus approach is ineffective.
They put forward counter-proposals of bottom-up governance.
At this same time this would lessen the emphasis on the UNFCCC.

The ___E:Kyoto Protocol U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kyoto_Protocol)___ to the UNFCCC adopted in 1997 set out legally binding emission reduction commitments for the "Annex 1" countries.  : 817 The Protocol defined three international policy instruments (" ___E:Flexibility Mechanisms U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flexibility_mechanisms)___ ") which could be used by the Annex 1 countries to meet their emission reduction commitments.
According to Bashmakov, use of these instruments could significantly reduce the costs for Annex 1 countries in meeting their emission reduction commitments.  : 402 [needs update]

The Paris Agreement reached in 2015 succeeded the ___E:Kyoto Protocol U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kyoto_Protocol)___ which expired in 2020. ___E:Countries that ratified the Kyoto protocol U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Kyoto_Protocol_signatories)___ committed to reduce their emissions of carbon dioxide and five other greenhouse gases, or engage in ___E:carbon emissions trading U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbon_emissions_trading)___ if they maintain or increase emissions of these gases.
In 2015, the UNFCCC's "structured expert dialogue" came to the conclusion that, "in some regions and vulnerable ecosystems, high risks are projected even for warming above 1.5 °C".

Together with the strong diplomatic voice of the poorest countries and the island nations in the Pacific, this expert finding was the driving force leading to the decision of the 2015 ___E:Paris Climate Conference U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_United_Nations_Climate_Change_Conference)___ to lay down this 1.5 °C long-term target on top of the existing 2 °C goal.
There are individual, institutional and market barriers to achieving climate change mitigation.  : 5–71 They differ for all the different mitigation options, regions and societies.
Difficulties with ___E:accounting for carbon dioxide removal U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbon_accounting)___ can act as economic barriers.

This would apply to BECCS ( ___E:bioenergy with carbon capture and storage U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bioenergy_with_carbon_capture_and_storage)___ ).  : 6–42 The strategies that companies follow can act as a barrier.
But they can also accelerate decarbonisation.  : 5–84

In order to decarbonise societies the state needs to play a predominant role. This is because it requires a massive coordination effort.  : 213 This strong government role can only work well if there is social cohesion, political stability and trust.  : 213
For land-based mitigation options, finance is a major barrier.
Other barriers are cultural values, governance, accountability and institutional capacity.  : 7–5
Developing countries face further barriers to mitigation.
One study estimates that only 0.12% of all funding for climate-related research goes on the social science of climate change mitigation.
Vastly more funding goes on natural science studies of climate change.
Considerable sums also go on studies of the impact of climate change and adaptation to it.
More than 1000 organisations with investments worth US$8 trillion have made commitments to ___E:fossil fuel divestment U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fossil_fuel_divestment)___ .

Socially responsible investing funds allow investors to invest in funds that meet high ___E:environmental, social and corporate governance U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Environmental,_social_and_corporate_governance)___ (ESG) standards.
The ___E:COVID-19 pandemic U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic)___ led some governments to shift their focus away from climate action, at least temporarily.
This obstacle to environmental policy efforts may have contributed to slowed investment in green energy technologies.
The economic slowdown resulting from COVID-19 added to this effect.
In 2020, carbon dioxide emissions fell by 6.4% or 2.3 billion tonnes globally.
Greenhouse gas emissions rebounded later in the pandemic as many countries began lifting restrictions.
The direct impact of pandemic policies had a negligible long-term impact on climate change.
The United States government has held shifting attitudes toward addressing greenhouse gas emissions.

The ___E:George W. Bush administration U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidency_of_George_W._Bush)___ opted not to sign the ___E:Kyoto Protocol U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kyoto_Protocol)___ ,  but the ___E:Obama administration U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Obama_administration)___ entered the ___E:Paris Agreement U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris_Agreement)___ .

The ___E:Trump administration U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_presidency_of_Donald_Trump)___ withdrew from the ___E:Paris Agreement U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris_Agreement)___ while increasing the export of ___E:crude oil U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crude_oil)___ and ___E:gas U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gasoline)___ , making the ___E:United States U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States)___ the largest producer.

China has committed to peak emissions by 2030 and reach ___E:net zero U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Net_zero)___ by 2060.  Warming cannot be limited to 1.5 °C if any ___E:coal plants in China U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electricity_sector_in_China#Coal_power)___ (without carbon capture) operate after 2045.  The ___E:Chinese national carbon trading scheme U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_national_carbon_trading_scheme)___ started in 2021.

The ___E:European Commission U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Commission)___ estimates that an additional €477 million in annual investment is needed for the European Union to meet its ___E:Fit-for-55 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fit_for_55)___ decarbonisation goals.

In the European Union, government-driven policies and the ___E:European Green Deal U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Green_Deal)___ have helped position greentech (as an example) as a vital area for venture capital investment.

By 2023, venture capital in the EU's greentech sector equalled that of the United States, reflecting a concerted effort to drive innovation and mitigate climate change through targeted financial support.

The European Green Deal has fostered policies that contributed to a 30% rise in venture capital for greentech companies in the EU from 2021 to 2023, despite a downturn in other sectors during the same period.
While overall venture capital investment in the EU remains about six times lower than in the United States, the greentech sector has closed this gap significantly, attracting substantial funding.
Key areas benefitting from increased investments are energy storage, circular economy initiatives, and agricultural technology.
This is supported by the EU's ambitious goal to reduce greenhouse gas emissions by at least 55% by 2030.

While ___E:solar radiation modification U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_geoengineering)___ (SRM) could reduce surface temperatures, it temporarily masks climate change rather than addressing the root cause, which is greenhouse gases.  : 14–56 SRM would work by altering how much solar radiation the Earth absorbs.  : 14–56 Examples include reducing the amount of sunlight reaching the surface, reducing the optical thickness and lifetime of clouds, and changing the ability of the surface to reflect radiation.

The ___E:IPCC U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intergovernmental_Panel_on_Climate_Change)___ describes SRM as a climate risk reduction strategy or supplementary option rather than a climate mitigation option.
The terminology in this area is still evolving.

Experts sometimes use the term geoengineering or ___E:climate engineering U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Climate_engineering)___ in the scientific literature for both CDR or SRM, if the techniques are used at a global scale.  : 6–11 IPCC reports no longer use the terms geoengineering or climate engineering .
